content: Herbal and plant-based treatments are frequently used for managing asthma, but there are ongoing concerns regarding their effectiveness and safety. In Western countries, individuals may turn to these treatments due to perceived safety or dissatisfaction with conventional medicine. In contrast, in China, herbal treatments are more commonly integrated into medical practice, and many conventional medications are derived from herbal sources. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of herbal and plant extracts in the treatment of chronic asthma. To achieve this, databases such as the Cochrane Airways Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and AMED were searched using predefined terms. The search was last updated in February 2007. The review included randomized, placebo-controlled trials that investigated any herbal or plant extract. Participants in these studies were required to have a primary diagnosis of asthma, and both adult and pediatric populations were eligible for inclusion. Two reviewers independently assessed the studies for their suitability, and data were extracted and cross-verified. A total of 27 studies, encompassing 29 experimental groups and involving 1,925 participants, met the inclusion criteria. These studies evaluated the effects of 21 different herbal preparations. However, the quality of the studies varied significantly, and many had small sample sizes. Regarding primary outcomes such as asthma exacerbations, steroid use, and lung function measurements, only two out of six studies reporting changes in FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in one second) showed positive results. Data on the frequency of asthma exacerbations were sparse, and one study that did report on this outcome found no benefit. Health-related quality of life was assessed in only one trial. The authors concluded that the evidence base for the use of herbal treatments in asthma is limited by the diversity of treatments studied, poor reporting quality, and insufficient data. The available evidence provides only a limited understanding of the long-term efficacy and safety of these treatments. Furthermore, the lack of standardized outcome measures reduces the reliability of the findings. While some positive results were observed, they highlight the need for additional well-designed clinical trials in this area.
